title: Every question within reach: building Wonder Agent with Gemma, LiteRT, and NVIDIA
gist: Wonder Agent (now Curilo Wonder) is a children's English-vocabulary app running Gemma 4 E2B/E4B, speech and image models fully on-device via LiteRT-LM, premised on driving the marginal cost of each learning interaction toward zero by eliminating per-request cloud inference. The write-up details INT8 quantization that cut SD-Turbo/SDXL-Turbo downloads ~74%, phone image-generation times (27–87 s) too slow for conversational use, NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada batch generation, and engineering lessons on latency measurement and tensor-buffer bugs.

insights.claim: Wonder Agent's thesis is that running Gemma and speech inference entirely on-device removes the per-request cloud inference bill, pushing the marginal cost of each additional learning interaction toward zero.
insights.speaker: Frank
insights.so_what: On-device inference shifts AI app unit economics from per-query cloud cost to one-time device/download cost, enabling free consumer AI apps.
insights.quote: Our vision is to bring the marginal cost of education closer to zero

insights.claim: The Wonder Agent team cautions that local inference only removes the per-request cloud bill; devices, electricity, downloads and development still cost money, and the app still uses the network for model provisioning, vocabulary refresh and voice downloads.
insights.speaker: Frank
insights.so_what: 'Offline AI' claims understate real costs and network dependence; evaluate total cost of ownership.

insights.claim: Wonder Agent won third place for Best Use of LiteRT, second place in the Mobile AI track and Best Use of Pixel / TPU at the Google Gemma Hardware Hackathon at AGI House, and is continuing as Curilo Wonder, a free not-for-profit app planned for Android and iOS.
insights.speaker: Frank
insights.so_what: Google is seeding an on-device Gemma developer ecosystem via hackathons.
insights.locator: Wonder Agent began as Frank's solo Android project

insights.claim: Wonder Agent uses Gemma 4 E2B/E4B via LiteRT-LM for transcription, explanations and image understanding, with separate offline TTS engines for speech and separate diffusion models for image generation.
insights.speaker: Frank
insights.so_what: A single small multimodal model can cover ASR plus reasoning on phones, reducing the number of on-device models needed.

insights.claim: Wonder Agent merged its separate transcribe and context-building steps after the hackathon to cut response time, reused one engine across requests to avoid re-initialisation, and caps replies at fifty spoken words since answer length drives waiting time.
insights.speaker: Frank
insights.so_what: Latency on edge LLM apps is won through pipeline design and output-length limits more than raw model speed.
insights.quote: answer length is a product decision that also affects waiting time
insights.locator: The hackathon pipeline reused the same engine

insights.claim: Wonder Agent's device validation recorded Gemma E2B running text on the Tensor G5 TPU with vision on GPU, but the team stresses this does not establish TPU support for every model or for diffusion pipelines.
insights.speaker: Frank
insights.so_what: Accelerator support on phones remains per-model and per-artifact; NPU fragmentation is a real deployment friction.

insights.claim: For on-device assistants, tokens-per-second is a poor proxy for user experience: a fast decode rate can coexist with long initialisation, and native time-to-first-token differs from when meaningful text or speech actually reaches the user.
insights.speaker: Frank
insights.so_what: Benchmarks of edge AI chips/runtimes that cite only tok/s can mislead; look for end-to-end latency metrics.
insights.quote: A fast decoding rate can coexist with a long initialization delay.

insights.claim: Wonder Agent's Research Lab benchmarks record model hashes, backend, runtime, device and thermal status, exclude warm-ups, and surface backend failures instead of silently falling back to CPU and labelling it an accelerator run.
insights.speaker: Frank
insights.so_what: Silent CPU fallback can inflate claimed accelerator performance — a diligence point for edge-AI benchmarks.

themes.theme: Image model quantization and phone performance

insights.claim: INT8 dynamic quantization of encoder/denoiser weights with FP16 VAE weights cut SD-Turbo runtime downloads from 5.03 GB to 1.32 GB (73.75%) and SDXL-Turbo from 13.75 GB to 3.53 GB (74.35%).
insights.speaker: Frank
insights.so_what: ~4x smaller diffusion bundles make on-phone image generation provisionable, though file size does not equal memory or speed.

insights.claim: On a Pixel 10 Pro Fold (Tensor G5) CPU, SD-Turbo INT8/FP16 generated a 512×512 one-step image in 26.92 s, FLUX.2 Klein 4B INT8 a 256×256 four-step image in 85.76 s, and SDXL-Turbo INT8/FP16 a 512×512 four-step image in 86.90 s, with peak RSS of 1.75–2.09 GiB.
insights.speaker: Frank
insights.so_what: On-phone diffusion is still far too slow for interactive use on CPU; mobile NPU/GPU support for diffusion is a gap to watch.
insights.locator: Phone measurements changed the product design

insights.claim: Because even ~27-second phone image generation is too slow for every conversational reply, Wonder Agent uses prepared illustrations and has Gemma caption images in the background, cancelling captioning when a new question arrives.
insights.speaker: Frank
insights.so_what: Product design must route around on-device generative latency; pre-computed assets remain essential.
insights.locator: For the product, the practical implication was clear

insights.claim: The compact SD exports failed GPU graph compilation on the tested Tensor G5 phone, even with only the denoiser on GPU, and image TPU execution requires separately compiled bundles.
insights.speaker: Frank
insights.so_what: Mobile GPU/TPU compiler coverage for diffusion models is immature — a bottleneck for on-device generative imaging.
insights.quote: Quantization solved a download problem; other runtime problems remained.

insights.claim: A tensor-buffer bug where exported text-encoder graphs exposed the input token tensor as a passthrough output caused failures that looked like model errors (bad conditioning in SD-Turbo, an out-of-bounds embedding abort in SDXL-Turbo); the fix was reusing shared input/output buffers.
insights.speaker: Frank
insights.so_what: Converted-model integration bugs are a hidden cost of edge deployment, favouring mature toolchains.
insights.locator: The bug between a converted model and a working phone

themes.theme: Cloud GPUs and coding agents in the edge workflow

insights.claim: An NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada workstation generated about 1.5 images per second for a 10,000-image presentation batch, versus roughly 180–360 seconds per image for the phone generation runs used at the time.
insights.speaker: Frank
insights.so_what: Even edge-first apps rely on workstation/cloud GPUs for content preparation — edge AI is complementary to datacenter GPU demand.

insights.claim: The team used Codex with the LiteRT CLI agent skill on a remote workstation to download, convert, quantize and package models, producing 5 public LiteRT model packages on Hugging Face that have been downloaded more than 5,000 times.
insights.speaker: Frank
insights.so_what: Coding agents with vendor 'skills' are becoming the interface for ML deployment toolchains — a lever for platform adoption.
insights.locator: Using Codex and the LiteRT skill
